```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.alt = "Visualization"
)
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
```

A transition network estimated from all sequences describes an average
process, which may describe none of the units that produced it.
Clustering divides the sequences into groups whose members resemble each
other more than they resemble the members of other groups, and a network
can then be estimated for each group (López-Pernas, Tikka & Saqr 2025).
Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas & Misiejuk 2026) clusters sequences by the
dissimilarity between them or with a mixture of Markov models, and turns
either clustering into one network per cluster.

| Step | Function |
|------|----------|
| Cluster by dissimilarity | `build_clusters()` |
| Compare numbers of clusters, distances and methods | `cluster_choice()` |
| Check a clustering | `cluster_diagnostics()` |
| Cluster with a mixture Markov model | `build_mmm()`, `cluster_mmm()`, `compare_mmm()` |
| One network per cluster | `build_network()` on a clustering |
| Clustering and networks in one call | `cluster_network()` |
| Compare the clusters' networks | `permutation()` |

## Data

`human_long` holds the coded human turns of 429 human-AI pair-programming
("vibe coding") sessions, one row per action, coded into three clusters of
codes: `Directive`, `Evaluative` and `Metacognitive`. The network holds one
sequence per session, ordered by `order_in_session`; the `timestamp`
column has the resolution of a day and would split the sessions that run
over two days. Sessions range from 1 to 164 actions. Vibe coding, programming by conversation with an AI assistant
(Sarkar & Drosos 2025), has been studied with transition networks and
sequence analysis (Saqr, Misiejuk & López-Pernas 2026; Misiejuk et al.
2026).

```{r data}
library(Nestimate)
net <- build_network(human_long, method = "tna", action = "cluster",
                     actor = "session_id", time = "order_in_session")
```

## Clustering by dissimilarity

`build_clusters()` computes a distance between every pair of sequences
and groups the sequences that are close (Saqr, López-Pernas, Helske, et
al. 2024). It takes the network, which stores the sequences, or the
sequences themselves. By default it uses the Hamming distance, the number
of positions at which two sequences differ (Hamming 1950), and partitions
the sequences around medoids (PAM; Kaufman & Rousseeuw 1990), each
cluster represented by its most central sequence.

```{r hamming}
clusters_hamming <- build_clusters(net, k = 3)
clusters_hamming
```

The print shows each cluster's size, mean within-cluster distance and
medoid, and the average silhouette width, which compares each sequence's
distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other one:
near 1 for well-separated clusters, near 0 for overlapping ones (Rousseeuw
1987). The three clusters hold 183, 106 and 140 sessions, with a
silhouette of 0.22.

`dissimilarity` selects the distance (Studer & Ritschard 2016):

| Distance | What it compares |
|----------|------------------|
| `hamming` | the states at each position |
| `lv`, `osa`, `dl` | the edits (insertions, deletions, substitutions, transpositions) that turn one sequence into the other |
| `lcs` | the longest common subsequence |
| `qgram`, `cosine`, `jaccard` | the patterns of q consecutive states the sequences contain |
| `jw` | the Jaro-Winkler similarity of the sequences as strings |

`method` selects the clustering: `"pam"` (default) or a hierarchical
clustering, which merges the closest sequences or groups step by step:
`"ward.D2"` (Ward's criterion, Ward 1963, as implemented by Murtagh &
Legendre 2014), `"ward.D"`, `"complete"`, `"average"`, `"single"`,
`"mcquitty"` and `"centroid"`. The Hamming distance can also weight the
positions (`weighted = TRUE`, with `lambda` setting how fast the weight
decays), so that early differences count more.

### Distance and sequence length

The Hamming and edit distances count positions or edits, so for sequences
of unequal length they are driven by length. `sequence_metrics()`
compares the clusters of a grouped network on any index, here the number
of actions (`valid_n`).

```{r hamming-length}
set.seed(2026)
sequence_metrics(build_network(clusters_hamming), indices = "valid_n")
```

The three Hamming clusters are sessions of about 10, 57 and 22 actions:
the clustering separates short, long and medium sessions. The cosine
distance compares the profiles of the patterns two sequences contain,
normalised by their length, and groups sessions by what they contain.

## Choosing the clustering

`cluster_choice()` fits every combination of `k`, `dissimilarity` and
`method` it is given and returns one row per configuration with the
average silhouette, the mean within-cluster distance, the cluster sizes
and the ratio of the largest to the smallest cluster; `<-- best` marks the
highest silhouette. Its `plot()` method draws the sweep as lines
(`type = "lines"`, silhouette against `k`), bars (`"bars"`, one per
configuration), a heatmap (`"heatmap"`), the trade-off between silhouette
and size ratio (`"tradeoff"`) or panels per method (`"facet"`).

### Number of clusters and method

```{r choice-k}
choice_k <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2:4, method = c("pam", "ward.D2",
                                                    "average"))
choice_k
plot(choice_k, type = "lines")
```

With the Hamming distance, the highest silhouettes (0.78) belong to
average linkage and Ward's criterion, which put 9 or 11 sessions in one
cluster and the rest in the other. A small cluster of very long sessions
lies far from everything else and raises the silhouette without describing
the data, which the size ratio (up to 420) shows. PAM gives balanced
clusters with lower silhouettes.

### Distance

```{r choice-distance}
choice_distance <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2,
                                  dissimilarity = c("hamming", "lv", "lcs",
                                                    "qgram", "cosine",
                                                    "jaccard"),
                                  method = "pam")
choice_distance
plot(choice_distance, type = "bars", abbrev = TRUE)
```

With two clusters and PAM, the Hamming, edit and longest-common-subsequence
distances have the highest silhouettes (0.49 to 0.50), and their clusters
are again separated by length. The cosine distance has a lower silhouette
(0.42) and the most balanced clusters (170 and 259 sessions).

### Cosine distance

```{r choice-cosine}
choice_cosine <- cluster_choice(net, k = 2:4, dissimilarity = "cosine",
                                method = c("pam", "ward.D2"))
choice_cosine
plot(choice_cosine, type = "tradeoff")
```

The trade-off plot places each configuration by its silhouette and its
size ratio; the preferred configurations are high and to the left. Two
clusters with PAM have the highest silhouette, 0.42, with clusters of 170
and 259 sessions. Three clusters with Ward's criterion have a similar
silhouette (0.42), but one of their clusters holds four sessions.

```{r clusters}
clusters <- build_clusters(net, k = 2, dissimilarity = "cosine")
clusters
```

## Diagnostics

`cluster_diagnostics()` reports one row per cluster for any clustering:
for a dissimilarity clustering the size, the mean within-cluster distance
and the silhouette, for a mixture Markov model the mixing share, the
average posterior probability and the classification error.

```{r diagnostics}
diagnostics <- cluster_diagnostics(clusters)
diagnostics
plot(diagnostics, type = "silhouette")
```

The second cluster is well separated (silhouette 0.56) and the first less
so (0.20); the silhouette plot shows some sessions of the first cluster
with negative values, closer to the other cluster than to their own.

```{r mds, fig.height = 5}
plot(clusters, type = "mds")
```

The multidimensional scaling plot places the sessions in two dimensions
so that their distances approximate the cosine distances, with a colour
and a shape per cluster. The second cluster is compact; the first spreads
widely.

## What the clusters contain

`sequence_plot()` draws the sessions of each cluster and the share of
each state at each position; `trim = 0.9` keeps the positions that hold
90% of the actions, since few sessions are long.

```{r clusters-index, fig.height = 5}
sequence_plot(clusters, type = "index", ncol = 2, nrow = 1, trim = 0.9)
```

```{r clusters-distribution}
sequence_plot(clusters, type = "distribution", ncol = 2, nrow = 1,
              trim = 0.9)
```

`sequence_metrics()` compares the clusters on the indices that describe
them.

```{r clusters-indices}
set.seed(2026)
sequence_metrics(build_network(clusters),
                 indices = c("valid_n", "transition_rate",
                             "longitudinal_entropy", "dominant_proportion"))
```

The first cluster (170 sessions) alternates between directives and
evaluations: it changes state more often (transition rate 0.57 against
0.44) and spreads its actions more evenly (entropy 0.85 against 0.70). The
second (259 sessions) is dominated by directives, which take 68% of a
session against 52% (`dominant_proportion`). The first cluster's sessions
are also longer (34 against 20 actions, Hedges' g = -0.61), so the clusters
differ in length as well as in content.

## Mixture Markov models

A mixture Markov model groups the sequences by their transitions: it fits
one Markov chain per cluster and assigns each sequence to the chain that
most probably generated it (Helske et al. 2024). `compare_mmm()` fits the
model for several numbers of clusters and compares them with the BIC
(Schwarz 1978), the AIC and the ICL (Biernacki, Celeux & Govaert 2000),
lower being better, and the average posterior probability of the assigned
cluster (AvePP). Each model is estimated from 50 random starts; `seed`
makes them reproducible.

```{r mmm-choice}
mixture_choice <- compare_mmm(net, k = 2:5, seed = 2026)
mixture_choice
plot(mixture_choice)
```

The BIC and the ICL are lowest with two clusters, which also have the
highest AvePP (0.80). The AIC keeps decreasing with more clusters, and the
five-cluster model does not converge.

```{r mmm}
mixture <- build_mmm(net, k = 2, seed = 2026)
mixture
```

In the first cluster (155 sessions) an evaluation is followed by another
evaluation with probability 0.47 and a directive by an evaluation with
probability 0.30. In the second (274 sessions) directives follow
directives (0.65) and metacognitive actions follow metacognitive actions
(0.31) more often. The model and the cosine clustering describe a similar
division: sessions that alternate between directing and evaluating, and
sessions that mostly direct.

```{r mmm-diagnostics}
mixture_diagnostics <- cluster_diagnostics(mixture)
mixture_diagnostics
plot(mixture_diagnostics, type = "posterior")
```

The average posterior probability is 0.83 in the first cluster and 0.77
in the second, and 20% of the sessions are expected to be misclassified.
The posterior plot shows each cluster's distribution of the sessions'
posterior probabilities; mass near 1 means clear assignments.

```{r mmm-sequences, fig.height = 5}
sequence_plot(mixture, type = "index", ncol = 2, nrow = 1, trim = 0.9)
```

`cluster_mmm()` fits the same model and returns the same `net_mmm`
object; it is the name under which the mixture model is reached from
`cluster_network()`.

## Networks per cluster

A clustering becomes one network per cluster in two ways.
`build_network()` on a clustering, from `build_clusters()` or
`build_mmm()`, estimates a network for each cluster from the clustered
sequences and returns a group of networks.

```{r networks-build}
cluster_networks <- build_network(clusters)
cluster_networks
```

```{r networks-plot, eval = has_cograph, fig.height = 5}
plot(cluster_networks)
```

`cluster_network()` does the clustering and the networks in one call:
`cluster_by` takes the clustering method (`"pam"`, a hierarchical method,
or `"mmm"` for the mixture model) and `dissimilarity` the distance.

```{r networks-shortcut}
one_call <- cluster_network(net, k = 2, cluster_by = "pam",
                            dissimilarity = "cosine")
one_call
cluster_diagnostics(one_call)
```

With the same settings, the two routes give the same clusters and the
same networks, and `cluster_diagnostics()` reads either. The two-step route
keeps the clustering as its own object, to plot its silhouettes or its
MDS projection and to describe the clusters before any network is
estimated; the one-call route goes straight to the networks.
`cluster_network()` builds the per-cluster networks afresh with the
network's method; `inherit = TRUE` also gives them the source network's
threshold, scaling and estimator settings. For the mixture model,
`cluster_network(net, k = 2, cluster_by = "mmm", seed = 2026)` and
`build_network(mixture)` return the fitted chains as networks.

```{r networks-mmm}
build_network(mixture)
```

## Comparing the clusters

`permutation()` compares the transition probabilities of the clusters
edge by edge, by shuffling the cluster labels of the sessions.

```{r comparison}
set.seed(2026)
permutation(cluster_networks, iter = 1000)
```

The clusters were formed to differ, so differences between their networks
are expected by construction; the test shows which transitions the
clusters differ in, not whether such groups exist in the population.
